**Suez Canal and the Suez Crisis (1956)**
The canal designed by Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened in 1869, which links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea and greatly shortened the voyage from Europe to India. In 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized it to pay for the Aswan High Dam, and Britain, France and Israel, which had secretly coordinated their plan in the Protocol of Sèvres, invaded in an Anglo-French operation code-named Musketeer. U.S. and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw, and a UN Emergency Force was then stationed in the Sinai.

**Gamal Abdel Nasser**
The leader of the Free Officers Movement, whose 1952 coup overthrew King Farouk; Farouk's infant son Fuad II was briefly king before the monarchy was abolished in 1953. As president, Nasser championed pan-Arab nationalism and Arab socialism and merged Egypt with Syria in the United Arab Republic (1958–1961).

**Anwar Sadat and the Camp David Accords**
Nasser's successor, who signed the 1978 Camp David Accords with Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin under the mediation of U.S. president Jimmy Carter. He was assassinated by Islamist soldiers during a 1981 Cairo military parade marking the anniversary of the 1973 crossing of the Suez Canal, an attack that also wounded his successor Hosni Mubarak.

**Operation Badr and the Yom Kippur War (1973)**
Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. In Operation Badr, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and used high-pressure water cannons to breach the sand ramparts of Israel's Bar-Lev Line, which earned Sadat the title "Hero of the Crossing." The fighting included the Battle of the Chinese Farm.

**Six-Day War and the Sinai Peninsula**
In 1967 Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, and Israel struck first, defeating Egypt, Syria and Jordan and capturing the entire Sinai Peninsula. Egypt regained the Sinai after the 1979 peace treaty that followed the Camp David Accords.

**Aswan High Dam and Lake Nasser**
The huge Nile dam built under Nasser with Soviet help after the U.S. and Britain withdrew their offer to fund it. Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, flooded ancient sites, so temples such as Abu Simbel were moved to higher ground.

**Pharaoh: crowns, crook and flail, and the Narmer Palette**
Pharaohs wore the white crown of Upper Egypt (hedjet), the red crown of Lower Egypt (deshret), or the two combined in the double crown (pschent), along with a false beard, the uraeus cobra and the crook and flail. The Narmer Palette shows King Narmer, possibly the same person as the legendary Menes, who is credited with unifying Egypt and founding Memphis, smiting an enemy with a mace; its other side shows two serpopards with intertwined necks.

**Hatshepsut**
The female pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty who ruled with, and then above, her stepson Thutmose III, and was depicted with a false beard. She sent a famous trading expedition to the land of Punt for frankincense and myrrh. After her death her name and images were erased from many monuments, and she was buried in tomb KV20 in the Valley of the Kings.

**Cleopatra VII and the Ptolemaic dynasty**
The Ptolemaic dynasty was founded by Ptolemy I, a general of Alexander the Great, after Alexander's conquest of Egypt. Its last ruler, Cleopatra VII, reportedly had herself smuggled to Julius Caesar rolled in a carpet; she allied with Mark Antony and killed herself after their defeat at Actium in 31 BCE. Octavian then had her son Caesarion executed and made Egypt a Roman province.

**Library of Alexandria and the Pharos lighthouse**
Alexander's city of Alexandria, whose street plan was said to have been marked out with barley flour, became the Ptolemies' capital. Its great library was catalogued in Callimachus's Pinakes and was partly burned during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria. The Lighthouse of Alexandria on the island of Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was later destroyed by earthquakes.

**Napoleon's Egyptian campaign (1798–1801)**
Napoleon invaded Egypt and defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids, where he reportedly told his troops that "forty centuries look down upon you." Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile (Aboukir Bay), and the scholars (savants) who came with the expedition produced the Description de l'Égypte. French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, a trilingual stele that later helped decipher hieroglyphics.

**Muhammad Ali Pasha**
The Ottoman Albanian officer who became ruler of Egypt in 1805 and broke the power of the Mamluks by massacring their leaders in 1811. He modernized the army and economy, built the Mahmudiyah Canal for year-round irrigation, and promoted cotton growing. His dynasty ruled Egypt until King Farouk was overthrown in 1952.

**British Egypt, Saad Zaghlul and the 1919 Revolution**
Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 and made it a protectorate in 1914; resentment grew after the 1906 Denshawai incident, in which villagers were harshly punished after a clash with British officers. The British exile of the nationalist leader Saad Zaghlul sparked the 1919 Revolution, and his Wafd Party led the push for independence, which Britain partly granted in 1922.

**Hosni Mubarak and Tahrir Square (2011)**
Sadat's successor, who ruled Egypt for about 30 years. Huge Arab Spring protests centered on Cairo's Tahrir Square forced him to resign in 2011, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi later took power after a 2013 coup.

**Manetho, the Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods**
Manetho was a priest of the Ptolemaic era who wrote a history that divided Egypt's rulers into the dynasties still used today; his list includes the possibly legendary queen Nitocris. Historians group these dynasties into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of disunity called Intermediate Periods. During the First Intermediate Period, the governors (nomarchs) of Egypt's 42 provinces, or nomes, gained power at the pharaohs' expense.
